issues.legal_issue: A suit for specific performance may be brought despite the absence of a prior exemption from restrictions on excess vacant land, with any decree made conditional on obtaining the required exemption.
material_facts: The agreement for sale did not fix a date for performance, and the seller later refused to perform it.
The purchaser argued that it had not sought specific performance earlier because no exemption had been obtained under the urban land ceiling law.
The purchaser had instead filed a suit seeking declaration of ownership and an injunction.
issues.conclusion: The absence of an exemption did not prevent the purchaser from filing a suit for specific performance; such a suit could have been brought and a conditional decree could have been made subject to obtaining the exemption.
issues.legal_principle: Section 20 of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976 did not bar the filing of a suit for specific performance concerning vacant land in excess of the ceiling limit. A conditional decree could be made subject to an exemption being obtained. The Court agreed with the Full Bench decision in Shah Jitendra Nanalal v. Patel Lallubhai Ishverbhai, AIR 1984 Guj 145.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The claimant brings a suit seeking enforcement of an agreement to sell land.
predicates.required_exemption_not_yet_obtained: The permission or exemption required before the land can be transferred has not yet been obtained.

issues.definition: When a claimant seeks specific performance of an agreement to sell land and the required exemption has not yet been obtained, the suit may proceed conditionally.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant who omits a specific-performance claim from a suit after the other party has clearly refused performance cannot later pursue that omitted claim on the same cause of action.
material_facts: The agreement fixed no date for performance.
The seller published a notice asserting ownership and possession and stating that the agreement and related authority had been cancelled.
After that notice, the purchaser filed a suit for declaration of ownership and an injunction but did not seek specific performance.
The purchaser later sought to add specific performance to the suit, rather than having included it when the refusal gave rise to a cause of action.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser had a cause of action for specific performance when the refusal was made clear, but its omission of that relief from the original suit amounted to relinquishment of that part of its claim and attracted the broad principles of Order 2 Rule 2 CPC.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 54 of the Limitation Act, 1963, when no date is fixed for performance, limitation for a suit for specific performance begins when the plaintiff has notice that performance is refused. Order 2 Rule 2 CPC embodies the principle that a claimant must include the whole claim arising from a cause of action; its broad, public-policy principles applied even though no later second suit had been filed.

rule.if: specific_performance_claim and refusal_known and no_performance_date_fixed and original_suit_omitted_performance

predicates.specific_performance_claim: The claimant seeks enforcement of an agreement to sell.
predicates.refusal_known: The claimant has notice that the other party refuses to perform the agreement.
predicates.no_performance_date_fixed: The agreement does not specify a date for performance.
predicates.original_suit_omitted_performance: After the cause of action arose, the claimant filed a suit concerning the same transaction but did not include a claim for specific performance.

issues.definition: If a claimant knows that performance has been refused under an agreement with no fixed performance date, and omits specific performance from a suit concerning the same transaction, the omitted claim is barred.

issues.legal_issue: An amendment adding a specific-performance claim after the limitation period cannot relate back when it changes the basis or character of the original suit.
material_facts: The purchaser's original suit sought declaration of ownership and an injunction, not specific performance.
The purchaser sought to add specific performance to the suit about eleven years after filing it.
The added relief substantially altered the character of the suit and increased its pecuniary jurisdiction, requiring transfer to another court.
issues.conclusion: The amendment could not relate back to the date of the original plaint to cure the limitation defect, and the specific-performance relief could not be granted.
issues.legal_principle: Article 54 of the Limitation Act, 1963 bars a specific-performance claim brought after the applicable period. In Vishwambhar v. Laxminarayan, (2001) 6 SCC 163, the Court held that an amendment changing the basis of a suit cannot relate back to cure a limitation defect. In K. Raheja Constructions Ltd. v. Alliance Ministries, 1995 Supp. (3) SCC 17, the Court held that a delayed amendment adding specific performance cannot defeat the other party's accrued limitation rights.

rule.if: pending_suit_amendment and amendment_adds_specific_performance and claim_out_of_time and amendment_changes_suit_character

predicates.pending_suit_amendment: A claimant seeks to amend a suit that is already pending.
predicates.amendment_adds_specific_performance: The amendment adds a claim to enforce an agreement to sell.
predicates.claim_out_of_time: The added claim is brought after the applicable limitation period has expired.
predicates.amendment_changes_suit_character: The added claim changes the basis or character of the original suit.

issues.definition: When an out-of-time amendment to a pending suit adds specific performance and changes the suit's character, it does not cure the limitation defect.

issues.legal_issue: The doctrine preventing inconsistent positions does not rescue a specific-performance claim that was not brought within the limitation period.
material_facts: The seller had earlier stated in proceedings and affidavits that the land had been sold and possession delivered to the purchaser.
The seller later published a notice asserting ownership and possession and stating that the agreement had been cancelled.
The purchaser relied on the seller's inconsistent positions but did not include specific performance in its suit after the refusal became clear.
issues.conclusion: The doctrines of election and approbation and reprobation did not assist the purchaser because it had failed to bring a suit for specific performance within the limitation period.
issues.legal_principle: C. Beepathumma v. V.S. Kadambolithaya, (1964) 5 SCR 836, discussed the doctrine of election in a different factual context. New Bihar Biri Leaves Co. v. State of Bihar, (1981) 1 SCC 537, applied approbation and reprobation to a party that accepted public-auction terms and later challenged them. Those decisions did not overcome the failure to sue for specific performance within the period in Article 54 of the Limitation Act, 1963.

predicates.specific_performance_claim: The claimant seeks enforcement of an agreement to sell.
predicates.opposing_party_took_inconsistent_positio: The opposing party earlier acted or stated that the agreement was being performed but later denied the claimant's rights or refused performance.
predicates.claimant_failed_to_sue_within_limitation: The claimant did not bring the specific-performance claim within the applicable limitation period after refusal became known.

issues.definition: If the opposing party took inconsistent positions but the claimant failed to sue for specific performance within limitation, those inconsistent positions do not save the claim.
